newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany bans rape in marriage after 25-year debate.
newsitem.headline: Germany bans rape in marriage after 25-year debate.

text.p: The German parliament on Thursday made rape within marriage a criminal offence, bringing Germany into line with most of its European Union partners after a quarter of a century of wrangling.
The statute book previously defined rape as extra-marital, meaning that a husband who raped his wife could be convicted only if he used violence to inflict bodily harm.
The cross-party bill, the fifth launched since 1972, was approved in a free vote without party constraint by an overwhelming 471 votes to 138.
It set a maximum jail sentence of 15 years for rapists and it widened the definition of rape to include sexual abuse apart from penetration.
It also used gender-neutral language to make rape of a man by either sex punishable and it acknowledged that someone could be forced into sex with emotional rather than physical violence.

"For a long time people said rape within marriage was just a peccadillo and that a wife had to be at her husband's disposal...The real scandal is that we have taken so long to do the obvious thing," said parliamentary speaker Rita Suessmuth.
"These injuries go much deeper than external hurt, they go to the deepest core of human personality," she told the assembly.

Women's Affairs Minister Claudia Nolte told North German Radio that it was "infinitely important to punish rape within marriage just the same way as rape outside marriage," adding: "Marriage is not a legal vacuum."

Politicians have reached broad agreement for several years on the need to recognise the crime, and the lower house even approved the measure a year ago. But wrangling over whether a wife should have the right to withdraw a complaint meant it failed to become law.
Nolte urged deputies not to let squabbles over a secondary issue block consensus this time on the cross-party draft.
The idea that, by marrying, a woman automatically consents to sex on demand with her husband was banished from the statute books of most Western European countries in the 1980s or early 1990s.

In a survey by Nolte's ministry, one-seventh of German women aged between 20 and 59 said they had been subjected at least once to rape or sexual coercion, three-quarters of them at the hands of a husband or partner.
Women in Germany are more likely to suffer sexual violence than any other kind of violent attack, robbery or burglary.

Most of the previous bills succumbed to conservative opposition led by the Christian Social Union, Chancellor Helmut Kohl's junior coalition partners from mostly-Catholic Bavaria, who saw the idea of marital rape as a feminist myth and a threat to family life.
The new bill picks up the demand of the centre-left opposition that a woman should not be allowed to withdraw a criminal complaint of rape against her husband.
The opposition argued that a wife was acutely vulnerable to pressure from her husband and protection from this pressure should take precedence over the need to allow for a reconciliation.
